Monte Carlo Portfolio Optimization¶

This notebook uses historical monthly returns from data/monthly_returns.csv to simulate and optimize a 30-stock portfolio. The analysis focuses on maximizing expected return and minimizing risk using Monte Carlo simulations and a constrained portfolio optimization step.

Objective and project goals¶

  • Use the existing S&P 500 equity universe and historical monthly return data.
  • Build a Monte Carlo simulation to explore the risk-return tradeoff.
  • Identify portfolios that maximize profit (expected return) while minimizing risk (volatility).
  • Compare random portfolios with an optimized allocation under full investment and long-only constraints.

Primer: Monte Carlo and the Risk Model¶

The Monte Carlo Approach¶

The core idea is simple: when a problem has too many moving parts for a clean analytical solution, just sample a ton of random inputs, evaluate each one, and see what the distribution looks like. For portfolio optimization, each "input" is a weight vector $w = (w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n)$, basically a decision about how to split every dollar across $n$ assets. We generate thousands of these weight vectors under realistic constraints (long-only, fully invested: $w_i \geq 0$, $\sum_i w_i = 1$), score each one on expected return and risk, and plot the cloud. Every portfolio an investor could hold under those rules lives somewhere in that cloud. The efficient frontier is just the upper-left edge, the set of portfolios where you can't get more return without taking on more risk.

How We Measure Risk¶

Following Markowitz (1952), risk here is annualized volatility, the standard deviation of portfolio returns, computed from the historical sample covariance matrix $\Sigma$ of the 30 assets:

$$ \sigma_p(w) \;=\; \sqrt{w^\top \Sigma \, w} \quad\text{(annualized by multiplying by }\sqrt{12}\text{ for monthly data)} $$

Volatility is a reasonable first-pass risk measure, but it's symmetric. It penalizes upside and downside equally, which isn't how most investors actually think about risk. So we cross-check with two asymmetric measures in the backtest: maximum drawdown (worst peak-to-trough loss) and bootstrap 5th-percentile terminal wealth (a downside-path measure that asks how bad things get in the left tail). The composite scoring metric for each portfolio is the Sharpe ratio $\mu_p(w) / \sigma_p(w)$, which collapses the return-vs-risk tradeoff onto a single axis. The constrained optimizer in Section 3 also enforces concentration risk controls, 10% caps per position and 30% caps per sector, to keep the optimizer from going all-in on a handful of historically overfit names.

Why Monte Carlo Fits This Problem¶

A few reasons this approach makes sense here:

  1. High-dimensional but bounded feasible region. Thirty assets under long-only / fully-invested constraints means weights live on the 29-dimensional simplex. There's no closed-form "best risk-return tradeoff" once you layer on realistic constraints, but the simplex itself is straightforward to sample uniformly.

  2. Built-in visualization of the tradeoff surface. A 50,000-point scatter plot colored by Sharpe ratio shows the entire risk-return landscape at a glance. That means the optimization result can be sanity-checked against the cloud. You don't have to take the optimizer's answer on faith.

  3. Constraints are trivial to enforce. Position caps, sector caps, whatever other inequality constraints you want. They're just accept/reject filters at sample time. No Lagrangian gymnastics needed.

  4. Natural pairing with bootstrap uncertainty quantification. The same sampling machinery that generates weight vectors can resample historical returns to answer: "if the next 10 years look like a reshuffle of the last 10, what's the distribution of terminal wealth?" That's exactly the uncertainty analysis the project proposal calls for.

  5. A strong baseline for the LP/QP track. The closed-form constrained optimum should always sit on the upper edge of the MC cloud. If it doesn't, something is wrong with the optimizer or the constraints. The MC sweep is the cheapest sanity check you can run.

From here, the notebook follows a standard pipeline: simulate, optimize under constraints, walk-forward backtest, benchmark against SPY and equal-weight, bootstrap for uncertainty, sweep inputs for sensitivity.

Monte Carlo simulation of random portfolios¶

A large sample of portfolios is generated with random long-only weights that sum to 1. Each portfolio is scored by expected return, volatility, and Sharpe ratio.

In [4]:
def random_weights(n):
    weights = np.random.random(n)
    return weights / np.sum(weights)

def portfolio_performance(weights, returns, cov):
    port_return = weights.dot(returns)
    port_vol = np.sqrt(weights.T @ cov @ weights)
    sharpe = port_return / port_vol if port_vol > 0 else 0.0
    return port_return, port_vol, sharpe

annual_returns = summary['Annual Return']
annual_cov = returns.cov() * 12

n_assets = len(annual_returns)

n_simulations = 50000
simulated = []
for _ in range(n_simulations):
    w = random_weights(n_assets)
    r, v, s = portfolio_performance(w, annual_returns.values, annual_cov.values)
    simulated.append((r, v, s, w))

sim_df = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        'Return': x[0],
        'Volatility': x[1],
        'Sharpe': x[2],
        'Weights': x[3]
    }
    for x in simulated
])

Constrained mean-variance optimization¶

The unconstrained MC cloud explores the feasible region under only long-only / fully-invested constraints. A typical investor also faces position-level and sector-level concentration limits. Here we solve for the true min-vol and max-Sharpe portfolios under additional realistic caps: at most 10% in any single name and at most 30% in any one sector.

In [7]:
sector_map = dict(zip(metadata['ticker'], metadata['sector']))
tickers = list(annual_returns.index)
sectors = sorted({sector_map[t] for t in tickers})
sector_idx = {s: [i for i, t in enumerate(tickers) if sector_map[t] == s]
              for s in sectors}

POSITION_CAP = 0.10
SECTOR_CAP = 0.30

def neg_sharpe(w, mu, cov):
    ret = w @ mu
    vol = np.sqrt(w @ cov @ w)
    return -ret / vol if vol > 0 else 0.0

def port_vol(w, cov):
    return np.sqrt(w @ cov @ w)

def optimize_portfolio(mu, cov, objective='max_sharpe',
                       position_cap=POSITION_CAP,
                       sector_cap=SECTOR_CAP,
                       sector_idx=None):
    n = len(mu)
    constraints = [{'type': 'eq', 'fun': lambda w: w.sum() - 1.0}]
    if sector_idx is not None and sector_cap is not None:
        for s, idxs in sector_idx.items():
            constraints.append({
                'type': 'ineq',
                'fun': lambda w, idxs=idxs: sector_cap - w[idxs].sum()
            })
    bounds = [(0, position_cap)] * n
    w0 = np.ones(n) / n
    if objective == 'max_sharpe':
        res = minimize(neg_sharpe, w0, args=(mu, cov), method='SLSQP',
                       bounds=bounds, constraints=constraints,
                       options={'ftol': 1e-9, 'maxiter': 500})
    elif objective == 'min_vol':
        res = minimize(port_vol, w0, args=(cov,), method='SLSQP',
                       bounds=bounds, constraints=constraints,
                       options={'ftol': 1e-9, 'maxiter': 500})
    else:
        raise ValueError(f'unknown objective: {objective}')
    return res.x

mu = annual_returns.values
cov = annual_cov.values

w_max_sharpe = optimize_portfolio(mu, cov, 'max_sharpe', sector_idx=sector_idx)
w_min_vol    = optimize_portfolio(mu, cov, 'min_vol',    sector_idx=sector_idx)

ms_ret, ms_vol, ms_sharpe = portfolio_performance(w_max_sharpe, mu, cov)
mv_ret, mv_vol, mv_sharpe = portfolio_performance(w_min_vol,    mu, cov)

print(f'Constrained max-Sharpe: return={ms_ret:.4f}  vol={ms_vol:.4f}  Sharpe={ms_sharpe:.4f}')
print(f'Constrained min-vol:    return={mv_ret:.4f}  vol={mv_vol:.4f}  Sharpe={mv_sharpe:.4f}')

Walk-forward backtest¶

Re-solve the constrained optimization at every rebalance using only the trailing 36-month training window, then record the realized return for the next month. This matches the walk-forward protocol described in the proposal and produces a true out-of-sample (OOS) track record.

In [10]:
TRAIN_MONTHS = 36
REBAL_MONTHS = 1

def walk_forward(returns_df, train_months, rebal_months, objective,
                 sector_idx, position_cap, sector_cap):
    realized_returns, dates, weights_history = [], [], []
    T = len(returns_df)
    n = returns_df.shape[1]
    for i in range(train_months, T, rebal_months):
        train = returns_df.iloc[i - train_months:i]
        mu_t = train.mean().values * 12
        cov_t = train.cov().values * 12
        try:
            w = optimize_portfolio(mu_t, cov_t, objective,
                                   position_cap=position_cap,
                                   sector_cap=sector_cap,
                                   sector_idx=sector_idx)
        except Exception:
            w = np.ones(n) / n  # fallback to equal-weight if solver fails
        end = min(i + rebal_months, T)
        period = returns_df.iloc[i:end]
        for j in range(len(period)):
            realized_returns.append(period.iloc[j].values @ w)
            dates.append(period.index[j])
            weights_history.append(w)
    return (pd.Series(realized_returns, index=dates),
            pd.DataFrame(weights_history, index=dates,
                         columns=returns_df.columns))

print('Running walk-forward backtest for max-Sharpe...')
ms_oos, ms_weights_oos = walk_forward(
    returns, TRAIN_MONTHS, REBAL_MONTHS, 'max_sharpe',
    sector_idx, POSITION_CAP, SECTOR_CAP)

print('Running walk-forward backtest for min-vol...')
mv_oos, mv_weights_oos = walk_forward(
    returns, TRAIN_MONTHS, REBAL_MONTHS, 'min_vol',
    sector_idx, POSITION_CAP, SECTOR_CAP)

eq_oos = returns.iloc[TRAIN_MONTHS:].mean(axis=1)

print(f'OOS period: {ms_oos.index[0].date()} -> {ms_oos.index[-1].date()} '
      f'({len(ms_oos)} months)')

In [13]:
def perf_metrics(r):
    months = len(r)
    total = (1 + r).prod()
    cagr = total ** (12 / months) - 1
    vol = r.std() * np.sqrt(12)
    sharpe = (r.mean() * 12) / vol if vol > 0 else 0
    eq = (1 + r).cumprod()
    dd = (eq / eq.cummax() - 1).min()
    return {'CAGR': cagr, 'Annual Vol': vol, 'Sharpe': sharpe, 'Max Drawdown': dd}

metrics_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Max-Sharpe (OOS)': perf_metrics(ms_oos),
    'Min-Vol (OOS)':    perf_metrics(mv_oos),
    'Equal-Weight':     perf_metrics(eq_oos),
    'S&P 500':          perf_metrics(spy_returns),
}).round(4)
print('Backtest performance metrics:')
metrics_df

Uncertainty & stress simulations¶

Two simulation flavors test how robust the MC-optimized portfolios are to different return paths:

5a. Historical bootstrap — resample the realized OOS monthly returns with replacement to generate alternative 10-year paths. Provides a distribution of terminal wealth and Sharpe under reshuffling.

5b. Regime-conditional bootstrap — split history into high-vol and low-vol regimes by rolling 3-month volatility of the equal-weight portfolio, then resample each regime separately. Probes behavior under different market conditions.

In [14]:
N_BOOT = 1000
HORIZON = 120  # 10-year horizon in months
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

def bootstrap_paths(series, n_paths, horizon, rng):
    n_months = len(series)
    vals = series.values
    terminal = np.empty(n_paths)
    sharpes  = np.empty(n_paths)
    for k in range(n_paths):
        idx = rng.integers(0, n_months, size=horizon)
        sample = vals[idx]
        terminal[k] = np.prod(1 + sample)
        ann_r = sample.mean() * 12
        ann_v = sample.std() * np.sqrt(12)
        sharpes[k] = ann_r / ann_v if ann_v > 0 else 0
    return terminal, sharpes

ms_terminal, ms_boot_sharpe = bootstrap_paths(ms_oos,       N_BOOT, HORIZON, rng)
eq_terminal, eq_boot_sharpe = bootstrap_paths(eq_oos,       N_BOOT, HORIZON, rng)
spy_terminal, spy_boot_sharpe = bootstrap_paths(spy_returns, N_BOOT, HORIZON, rng)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
axes[0].hist(ms_terminal,  bins=50, alpha=0.6, label='Max-Sharpe',   color='steelblue')
axes[0].hist(eq_terminal,  bins=50, alpha=0.6, label='Equal-Weight', color='darkorange')
axes[0].hist(spy_terminal, bins=50, alpha=0.6, label='S&P 500',      color='dimgray')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Terminal wealth (10yr horizon)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Frequency')
axes[0].set_title(f'Bootstrap: terminal wealth distribution (n={N_BOOT})')
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].hist(ms_boot_sharpe,  bins=50, alpha=0.6, label='Max-Sharpe',   color='steelblue')
axes[1].hist(eq_boot_sharpe,  bins=50, alpha=0.6, label='Equal-Weight', color='darkorange')
axes[1].hist(spy_boot_sharpe, bins=50, alpha=0.6, label='S&P 500',      color='dimgray')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Sharpe ratio')
axes[1].set_title('Bootstrap: Sharpe distribution')

                                np.median(eq_terminal),

                                np.percentile(eq_terminal, 5),

def bootstrap_regime(r, n_paths=1000, horizon=12, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng(42)
    if len(r) == 0:
        return np.array([])
    vals = r.values
    means = np.empty(n_paths)
    for k in range(n_paths):
        idx = rng.integers(0, len(vals), size=horizon)
        means[k] = vals[idx].mean() * 12
    return means

rng2 = np.random.default_rng(7)

ms_low_dist  = bootstrap_regime(ms_low,  rng=rng2)
eq_high_dist = bootstrap_regime(eq_high, rng=rng2)
eq_low_dist  = bootstrap_regime(eq_low,  rng=rng2)

Sensitivity analysis¶

The walk-forward results above use a fixed configuration: 10% position cap, 30% sector cap, 36-month training window, max-Sharpe objective. This section sweeps each input independently and re-runs the full walk-forward backtest. The goal is to (a) verify the headline conclusion is not an artifact of a single tuning choice and (b) surface which knobs actually move out-of-sample performance.

For each parameter sweep we record OOS CAGR, annualized volatility, Sharpe, max drawdown, and average monthly turnover.

In [17]:
# Sensitivity helpers: re-run walk_forward() under perturbed inputs and summarize OOS performance.

def oos_stats(r, weights_df=None):
    """Compute the OOS performance row used in all sensitivity sweeps."""
    m = perf_metrics(r)
    if weights_df is not None and len(weights_df) > 1:
        m['Turnover'] = weights_df.diff().abs().sum(axis=1).mean()
    else:
        m['Turnover'] = np.nan
    return m

def run_sensitivity(returns_df, *, train_months=TRAIN_MONTHS, rebal_months=REBAL_MONTHS,
                    objective='max_sharpe', position_cap=POSITION_CAP,
                    sector_cap=SECTOR_CAP, sector_idx=sector_idx,
                    mu_shrinkage=0.0):
    """Walk-forward backtest with an optional mu-shrinkage perturbation.

    mu_shrinkage in [0, 1]: 0 = raw sample mean, 1 = grand mean (full shrinkage).
    """
    realized, dates, weights_history = [], [], []
    T = len(returns_df)
    n = returns_df.shape[1]
    for i in range(train_months, T, rebal_months):
        train = returns_df.iloc[i - train_months:i]
        mu_t = train.mean().values * 12
        if mu_shrinkage > 0:
            mu_t = (1 - mu_shrinkage) * mu_t + mu_shrinkage * mu_t.mean()
        cov_t = train.cov().values * 12
        try:
            w = optimize_portfolio(mu_t, cov_t, objective,
                                   position_cap=position_cap,
                                   sector_cap=sector_cap,
                                   sector_idx=sector_idx)
        except Exception:
            w = np.ones(n) / n
        end = min(i + rebal_months, T)
        period = returns_df.iloc[i:end]
        for j in range(len(period)):
            realized.append(period.iloc[j].values @ w)
            dates.append(period.index[j])
            weights_history.append(w)
    r = pd.Series(realized, index=dates)
    w_df = pd.DataFrame(weights_history, index=dates, columns=returns_df.columns)
    return r, w_df

** Sensitivity Takeaways **

Ranking parameters by how much they move OOS Sharpe across the sweep (see tornado chart):

Training window has the largest spread (0.92 to 1.27, range 0.35). But OOS lengths differ across rows (107 down to 59 months), so part of that spread is just window selection. A 12-month train starts the OOS in 2017 and picks up the favorable 2017-2019 stretch; the 60-month train starts in 2021 and absorbs the 2022 drawdown without earlier gains to offset. The honest read: performance is roughly flat from 36 to 48 months and decays at both extremes once you account for the bias/variance tradeoff. The 36-month default holds up fine. Position cap is the most actionable knob (spread 0.29). Tighter caps (5%) push the portfolio toward equal-weight and produce a higher OOS Sharpe (1.24), lower turnover (0.10 vs 0.22), and a smaller drawdown (-25%). Remove the cap entirely and estimation error concentrates the book: Sharpe collapses to 0.96 with a -38% drawdown. A 5-7.5% cap would dominate the current 10% on every metric. Sector cap basically doesn't matter at the current position cap (spread 0.03). The 30%, 40%, 50%, and 100% rows are identical to four decimals. With 10% per-name limits already in place, the sector constraint is slack in every OOS window. Only the tightest setting (20%) nudges Sharpe up to 1.13. The two caps are partial substitutes; only the tighter one is doing real work. Mu shrinkage is a risk lever, not a Sharpe lever (spread 0.02). Sharpe is nearly flat across λ ∈ [0, 1], but volatility drops from 17.5% to 13.9% and max drawdown from -29% to -17%. At λ=1, the max-Sharpe portfolio numerically converges to the min-vol portfolio (compare to Section 4). Shrinking μ doesn't generate higher risk-adjusted returns here. It produces a lower-risk portfolio at roughly the same Sharpe.

Implication for the writeup. The headline ranking from Section 4 (equal-weight > walk-forward portfolios > SPY on Sharpe) is robust. No setting in any sweep flips it. The two practical improvements the sensitivity analysis surfaces:

Tighten the position cap to 5-7.5%. Best OOS Sharpe (1.24), lowest turnover (0.10), smallest drawdown (-25%) across the position-cap sweep. Drop the sector cap or fold it into a single tighter position cap. It adds no value at the current 10% per-name limit.

Constrained CVaR Optimization¶

Max-Sharpe and Min-Vol both treat upside and downside symmetrically. They care about variance, not about which side of the mean the returns fall on. The regime analysis in Section 5b showed why this matters: the max-Sharpe portfolio earns 15.3% annualized in high-vol months vs 24.8% in low-vol months, giving back more in stress periods than a balanced book would.

CVaR (Conditional Value at Risk, also called Expected Shortfall) takes a different approach. It explicitly minimizes the average loss in the worst tail of outcomes. At confidence level $\alpha$:

$$\mathrm{CVaR}_\alpha(w) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[\, L(w) \,\bigm|\, L(w) \geq \mathrm{VaR}_\alpha(w) \,\right], \qquad L(w) = -w^\top r$$

CVaR is asymmetric (only counts losses), coherent (subadditive, unlike VaR), and, critically for this project, has an exact LP formulation (Rockafellar & Uryasev 2000). Given $J$ historical return scenarios $r_j$, the optimization

$$\min_{w,\zeta,u} \;\; \zeta + \tfrac{1}{J(1-\alpha)} \sum_{j=1}^J u_j \quad\text{s.t.}\quad u_j \geq -w^\top r_j - \zeta,\;\; u_j \geq 0,\;\; \sum_i w_i = 1,\;\; 0 \leq w_i \leq \text{cap}$$

is a linear program in $(w, \zeta, u)$. No QP or SLSQP needed. At the optimum, $\zeta = \mathrm{VaR}_\alpha$ and the objective value equals $\mathrm{CVaR}_\alpha$.

This bridges the MC track to the LP track and gives a third comparable strategy in the final summary.

Caveat on sample size. With a 36-month training window and $\alpha = 0.95$, only $\lfloor (1-\alpha) J \rfloor \approx 2$ scenarios sit at or below VaR per refit, so the per-window CVaR estimate is noisy. The OOS performance below is what matters. The in-sample CVaR is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.

In [24]:
from scipy.optimize import linprog

ALPHA = 0.95  # CVaR confidence level (worst 5% of months)

def optimize_cvar(scenarios, alpha=ALPHA,
                  position_cap=POSITION_CAP, sector_cap=SECTOR_CAP,
                  sector_idx=None):
    """Minimize CVaR_alpha via the Rockafellar-Uryasev LP.

    scenarios: (J, n) array of historical return rows.
    Returns the weight vector that minimizes expected loss in the worst (1-alpha) tail.
    """
    J, n = scenarios.shape
    n_vars = n + 1 + J  # w (n), zeta (1), u (J)

    # Objective: min zeta + (1/(J*(1-alpha))) * sum(u_j)
    c = np.zeros(n_vars)
    c[n] = 1.0
    c[n + 1:] = 1.0 / (J * (1 - alpha))

    # u_j >= -r_j @ w - zeta  ->  -r_j @ w - zeta - u_j <= 0
    A_ub = np.zeros((J, n_vars))
    A_ub[:, :n] = -scenarios
    A_ub[:, n] = -1.0
    A_ub[np.arange(J), n + 1 + np.arange(J)] = -1.0
    b_ub = np.zeros(J)

    # Sector caps: sum_{i in s} w_i <= sector_cap
    if sector_idx is not None and sector_cap is not None:
        for _, idxs in sector_idx.items():
            row = np.zeros(n_vars)
            row[idxs] = 1.0
            A_ub = np.vstack([A_ub, row])
            b_ub = np.append(b_ub, sector_cap)

    # Equality: sum(w) = 1
    A_eq = np.zeros((1, n_vars))
    A_eq[0, :n] = 1.0
    b_eq = np.array([1.0])

    bounds = ([(0, position_cap)] * n
              + [(None, None)]      # zeta free
              + [(0, None)] * J)    # u >= 0

    res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub, A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=b_eq,
                  bounds=bounds, method='highs')
    if not res.success:
        raise RuntimeError(f'CVaR LP failed: {res.message}')
    return res.x[:n]


# In-sample CVaR-min on the full history

cvar_ret, cvar_vol, cvar_sharpe = portfolio_performance(w_cvar, mu, cov)

# Realized in-sample tail metrics

      f'return={cvar_ret:.4f}  vol={cvar_vol:.4f}  Sharpe={cvar_sharpe:.4f}')

def walk_forward_cvar(returns_df, train_months, rebal_months, alpha,
                      sector_idx, position_cap, sector_cap):
    """CVaR-min walk-forward backtest. Same protocol as walk_forward()."""
    realized, dates, weights_history = [], [], []
    T = len(returns_df)
    n = returns_df.shape[1]
    for i in range(train_months, T, rebal_months):
        train = returns_df.iloc[i - train_months:i].values
        try:
            w = optimize_cvar(train, alpha=alpha,
                              position_cap=position_cap,
                              sector_cap=sector_cap,
                              sector_idx=sector_idx)
        except Exception:
            w = np.ones(n) / n  # equal-weight fallback if LP fails
        end = min(i + rebal_months, T)
        period = returns_df.iloc[i:end]
        for j in range(len(period)):
            realized.append(period.iloc[j].values @ w)
            dates.append(period.index[j])
            weights_history.append(w)
    return (pd.Series(realized, index=dates),
            pd.DataFrame(weights_history, index=dates,
                         columns=returns_df.columns))


print(f'Running walk-forward backtest for CVaR{int(ALPHA*100)}-min...')
cvar_oos, cvar_weights_oos = walk_forward_cvar(
    returns, TRAIN_MONTHS, REBAL_MONTHS, ALPHA,
    sector_idx, POSITION_CAP, SECTOR_CAP)

cvar_turnover = cvar_weights_oos.diff().abs().sum(axis=1).mean()
print(f'OOS period: {cvar_oos.index[0].date()} -> {cvar_oos.index[-1].date()} '
      f'({len(cvar_oos)} months)')
print(f'Average monthly turnover (CVaR-min): {cvar_turnover:.3f}')


# Tail-risk comparison across all walk-forward strategies + benchmarks
def tail_metrics(r, alpha=ALPHA):
    losses = -r.values
    var = np.quantile(losses, alpha)
    cvar = losses[losses >= var].mean()
    return var, cvar

tail_rows = []
for name, series in [
    ('Max-Sharpe (OOS)', ms_oos),
    ('Min-Vol (OOS)',    mv_oos),
    ('CVaR-min (OOS)',   cvar_oos),
    ('Equal-Weight',     eq_oos),
    ('S&P 500',          spy_returns),
]:
    v, c_ = tail_metrics(series)
    m = perf_metrics(series)
    tail_rows.append({
        'Strategy': name,
        'CAGR':         m['CAGR'],
        'Ann Vol':      m['Annual Vol'],
        'Sharpe':       m['Sharpe'],
        'Max DD':       m['Max Drawdown'],
        f'VaR{int(ALPHA*100)} (monthly)':  v,
        f'CVaR{int(ALPHA*100)} (monthly)': c_,
    })
tail_df = pd.DataFrame(tail_rows).set_index('Strategy').round(4)
print('OOS performance + tail-risk metrics (VaR / CVaR are monthly loss, positive = loss):')
tail_df

# CVaR alpha-sensitivity. At alpha=0.95 with a 36-mo training window only ~2 scenarios
# sit below VaR, so CVaR-min partly collapses toward Min-Vol. Sweep alpha to see how the
# choice of tail depth moves OOS behavior.
alpha_grid = [0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99]
alpha_rows = []
for a in alpha_grid:
    r_oos, w_oos = walk_forward_cvar(returns, TRAIN_MONTHS, REBAL_MONTHS, a,
                                     sector_idx, POSITION_CAP, SECTOR_CAP)
    m = perf_metrics(r_oos)
    var_a, cvar_a = tail_metrics(r_oos, alpha=a)
    alpha_rows.append({
        'alpha': a,
        'Scenarios below VaR (train)': int((1 - a) * TRAIN_MONTHS),
        'CAGR':     m['CAGR'],
        'Ann Vol':  m['Annual Vol'],
        'Sharpe':   m['Sharpe'],
        'Max DD':   m['Max Drawdown'],
        f'VaR (monthly)':  var_a,
        f'CVaR (monthly)': cvar_a,
        'Turnover': w_oos.diff().abs().sum(axis=1).mean(),
    })
alpha_df = pd.DataFrame(alpha_rows).round(4)
print('CVaR-min alpha sensitivity (OOS, VaR/CVaR measured at the same alpha as the optimizer):')
alpha_df

How this maps to the project proposal¶

  • Walk training window forward one period at a time — Section 3 (36mo train / 1mo rebal, matching the data-pipeline notebook config).
  • Use various simulations to understand uncertainty in our model — Section 5a (historical bootstrap of OOS returns).
  • Test optimal portfolios under various market conditions — Section 5b (regime-conditional bootstrap, high-vol vs low-vol).
  • Compare against various benchmarks (i.e. S&P 500) — Section 4 (SPY equity-curve overlay + metrics table) and Section 6 (summary).
  • Back-test against historical performance — Sections 3-4 produce the full OOS track record. The constrained LP allocations from Scott's notebook can be added as additional rows in the Section 6 summary.

Key Findings¶

Mapping to the project proposal¶

Each deliverable from the proposal maps to a specific section of the notebook:

  • Walk training window forward one period at a time: Section 3 (36-month train / 1-month rebalance, matching the data-pipeline notebook config).
  • Use various simulations to understand uncertainty in our model: Section 5a (historical bootstrap of OOS returns).
  • Test optimal portfolios under various market conditions: Section 5b (regime-conditional bootstrap, high-vol vs low-vol).
  • Compare against various benchmarks (i.e. S&P 500): Section 4 (SPY equity-curve overlay + metrics table) and Section 6 (summary).
  • Back-test against historical performance: Sections 3-4 produce the full OOS track record. The constrained LP allocations from Scott's notebook can be added as additional rows in the Section 6 summary.

What the results show¶

1. Constraints matter. The constrained optimum beats the random MC max-Sharpe. The unconstrained MC sweep finds a best Sharpe of 1.52 (in-sample). Imposing realistic concentration limits (10% per name, 30% per sector) and solving with SLSQP raises the best in-sample Sharpe to 1.70. The MC cloud only samples random feasible points. It does not search the boundary efficiently.

2. Estimation error kills the in-sample edge. The constrained max-Sharpe portfolio falls from Sharpe 1.70 in-sample to Sharpe 1.10 out-of-sample under monthly walk-forward rebalancing. The optimizer overfits noisy 36-month estimates of μ and Σ. This is the classic Markowitz overfit story and is the single most important takeaway for the writeup.

3. Equal-weight is the toughest benchmark, not SPY. Out-of-sample (June 2019 to April 2026, 83 months):

Strategy CAGR Vol Sharpe Max DD
Walk-fwd Max-Sharpe 19.2% 17.5% 1.10 -28.7%
Walk-fwd Min-Vol 15.5% 13.9% 1.11 -17.2%
Equal-Weight 21.5% 16.8% 1.26 -19.9%
S&P 500 (SPY) 16.6% 17.0% 0.99 -24.0%

Both walk-forward portfolios beat SPY on Sharpe, but equal-weight beats both. Naive diversification across the 30-asset universe is a strong baseline, consistent with DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009).

4. Min-vol delivers what it promises. It has the lowest realized volatility (13.9%) and the smallest drawdown (-17.2%) of any strategy tested. A risk-averse investor is well served by the walk-forward min-vol formulation, even if its Sharpe is similar to max-Sharpe.

5. Bootstrap confirms the OOS ranking is robust. Across 1,000 resampled 10-year paths, the median terminal wealth ranks Equal-Weight (6.9×) > Max-Sharpe (5.8×) > SPY (4.7×). The 5th-percentile (downside) wealth multiples preserve the same order, so the ranking is not driven by a single lucky path.

6. The max-Sharpe portfolio underperforms in high-vol regimes. Splitting the 83 OOS months by rolling 3-month volatility (median split: 51 high-vol months / 32 low-vol months):

  • Max-Sharpe earns 15.3% annualized in high-vol months vs 24.8% in low-vol months.
  • Equal-Weight earns 17.6% vs 27.4%, also down but holds up better than max-Sharpe.

The concentration the optimizer prefers (10% caps tend to bind on a handful of names) hurts more when those names sell off together. This is direct evidence for "test optimal portfolios under various market conditions" from the proposal.

7. Turnover is reasonable. Average monthly turnover for the walk-forward max-Sharpe portfolio is 0.22 (sum of absolute weight changes per rebalance). At 10 bps per side that would shave roughly 0.4% off annual returns. Material but not catastrophic, so transaction costs would not overturn the ranking above.

Sensitivity takeaways¶

Ranking parameters by how much they move OOS Sharpe across the sweep (see tornado chart):

  • Training window has the largest spread (0.92 to 1.27, range 0.35). But OOS lengths differ across rows (107 down to 59 months), so part of that spread is just window selection. A 12-month train starts the OOS in 2017 and picks up the favorable 2017-2019 stretch; the 60-month train starts in 2021 and absorbs the 2022 drawdown without earlier gains to offset. The honest read: performance is roughly flat from 36 to 48 months and decays at both extremes once you account for the bias/variance tradeoff. The 36-month default holds up fine.

  • Position cap is the most actionable knob (spread 0.29). Tighter caps (5%) push the portfolio toward equal-weight and produce a higher OOS Sharpe (1.24), lower turnover (0.10 vs 0.22), and a smaller drawdown (-25%). Remove the cap entirely and estimation error concentrates the book: Sharpe collapses to 0.96 with a -38% drawdown. A 5-7.5% cap would dominate the current 10% on every metric.

  • Sector cap basically doesn't matter at the current position cap (spread 0.03). The 30%, 40%, 50%, and 100% rows are identical to four decimals. With 10% per-name limits already in place, the sector constraint is slack in every OOS window. Only the tightest setting (20%) nudges Sharpe up to 1.13. The two caps are partial substitutes; only the tighter one is doing real work.

  • Mu shrinkage is a risk lever, not a Sharpe lever (spread 0.02). Sharpe is nearly flat across λ ∈ [0, 1], but volatility drops from 17.5% to 13.9% and max drawdown from -29% to -17%. At λ=1, the max-Sharpe portfolio numerically converges to the min-vol portfolio (compare to Section 4). Shrinking μ doesn't generate higher risk-adjusted returns here. It produces a lower-risk portfolio at roughly the same Sharpe.

Implications for the writeup¶

  • Frame the MC track as a stress test of the LP/QP allocations, not as a stand-alone strategy: equal-weight as the headline benchmark, SPY as the secondary benchmark, walk-forward portfolios as the candidate strategies.
  • Estimation risk is the central theme. The proposal asked for "uncertainty in our model." Quantify it with the in-sample/OOS gap (1.70 to 1.10 Sharpe) and the bootstrap percentile bands.
  • The sensitivity analysis surfaces two practical improvements: tighten the position cap to 5-7.5% (best OOS Sharpe, lowest turnover, smallest drawdown) and drop the sector cap or fold it into a single tighter position cap (it adds no value at the current 10% per-name limit).
  • When Scott's LP allocations land, run them through the same walk_forward() + perf_metrics() + bootstrap_paths() pipeline so the comparison is apples-to-apples.

Glossary of terms and abbreviations¶

A reference for the terminology and shorthand used throughout this notebook.

Optimization & solver¶

Term Definition
LP Linear Programming — optimization with a linear objective and linear constraints.
QP Quadratic Programming — quadratic objective (e.g., portfolio variance) with linear constraints. Markowitz mean-variance is a QP.
MC Monte Carlo — sampling-based simulation; here, drawing random weight vectors to explore the feasible region.
SLSQP Sequential Least Squares Programming — the nonlinear solver (via scipy.optimize.minimize) used for the constrained optimization.
Objective function The quantity being maximized or minimized (here, Sharpe ratio or portfolio volatility).
Constraint Restriction on feasible solutions: long-only ($w_i \geq 0$), fully invested ($\sum_i w_i = 1$), position cap, sector cap.
Simplex (29-dim) The geometric set of all long-only, fully-invested weight vectors over 30 assets.
Feasible region Subset of the simplex satisfying every constraint (position cap, sector cap, etc.).

Portfolio construction¶

Term Definition
w Weight vector — fraction of capital allocated to each asset, $w = (w_1, \ldots, w_n)$.
μ (mu) Vector of per-asset expected (annualized) returns.
Σ (Sigma) Covariance matrix of asset returns; diagonal is variances, off-diagonal is pairwise covariances.
Long-only No short positions allowed ($w_i \geq 0$).
Fully invested Weights sum to one ($\sum_i w_i = 1$); no cash held.
Position cap Maximum weight in any single asset (baseline: 10%). Controls name-level concentration.
Sector cap Maximum total weight in any one GICS sector (baseline: 30%). Controls sector-level concentration.
Equal-weight (EW) Naive baseline allocating $1/n$ to each asset; a strong benchmark per DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009).
Rebalance Re-solving the optimization and resetting weights to the new target (monthly here).
Turnover Sum of absolute weight changes between consecutive rebalances; proxy for trading cost.

Risk & performance metrics¶

Term Definition
σ_p (volatility) Portfolio standard deviation, $\sigma_p = \sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}$. Annualized by $\sqrt{12}$ for monthly data.
Sharpe ratio Risk-adjusted return: $\mu_p / \sigma_p$ (risk-free rate set to 0 here).
CAGR Compound Annual Growth Rate: $(1 + \text{total return})^{12/\text{months}} - 1$.
Max drawdown (DD) Largest peak-to-trough decline in cumulative wealth. Asymmetric downside risk measure.
MAD Mean Absolute Deviation — LP-compatible risk measure (used in the LP track, not here).
Terminal wealth Cumulative wealth multiple at the end of a simulated path (e.g., 6.9× starting capital).

Evaluation protocol¶

Term Definition
OOS Out-of-Sample — performance computed on data not used to fit weights.
In-sample Performance computed using the same data the optimizer was fit on; optimistically biased.
Walk-forward backtest Rolling-window OOS evaluation: fit on the trailing 36 months, hold for 1 month, advance, repeat.
Training window Length of the trailing return history used to estimate μ and Σ (baseline: 36 months).
Bootstrap Resampling with replacement from historical returns to generate alternative paths and quantify uncertainty.
Regime-conditional bootstrap Bootstrap stratified by market state (here, high-vol vs low-vol months by rolling 3-mo volatility).
μ shrinkage (λ) Pulling sample means toward the cross-sectional grand mean: $\mu' = (1-\lambda)\mu + \lambda \bar{\mu}$. Reduces estimation error.

Strategies referenced¶

Term Definition
Max-Sharpe Portfolio maximizing $\mu_p / \sigma_p$ subject to constraints.
Min-vol Portfolio minimizing $\sigma_p$ subject to constraints.
MPT Modern Portfolio Theory — Markowitz (1952) mean-variance framework.

Data & external¶

Term Definition
S&P 500 Standard & Poor's 500 index of large-cap US equities; benchmark for this project.
SPY SPDR S&P 500 ETF — tradable proxy for the S&P 500 used in the benchmark comparison.
GICS Global Industry Classification Standard — the sector taxonomy used for the sector cap.
yfinance Python wrapper around Yahoo Finance market data; source of price history.
Adjusted close Closing price adjusted for dividends and splits; basis for the monthly returns.
